The announcement of more than 14 million euros for the Italian border territories, with resources that also reach the municipalities of Varesotto, rekindles the spotlight on the system of tax refunds linked to border workers. The news, reported by Luino Notizie, is part of the implementation of the New Agreement between Italy and Switzerland on frontier workers, signed on 23 December 2020 and entered into force on 1 January 2024 after Italian ratification with Law 83 of 13 June 2023.
### The refreshment mechanism in the new framework The refreshment system provides that a portion of the tax at source withheld in Switzerland on the income of border workers is paid to the Italian municipalities of residence. For the Italian municipalities of Varesotto and Alto Verbano, these resources feed the ordinary budget: road maintenance, social services, school and local public transport. For border crossers residing in thisarea, the flow of refunds is the territorial consideration of the tax they pay in Switzerland.

## Key facts - **What**: Evolution of banking supervision and financial scandals. - When: From 1935 to the present, with a focus on 1965, 1977 and 1984. - Where: Switzerland, with international impact. - Who: CFB, Finma, BNS, SBS, UBS. - Amount: 3 billion francs of support in 1977.
The history of Swiss banking supervision is a tormented one, marked by a constant tension between the need for strict controls and the influence of the financial lobby. The regulatory framework took its first steps after the economic crisis of the 1930s, driven by the bankruptcy of the Banque de Genève in 1931 and the difficulties of the Swiss People's Bank. On March 1, 1935, the Federal Law on Banks and Savings Banks came into force, giving rise to the Federal Commission of Banks (CFB), an independent body in charge of monitoring the liquidity and own funds of institutions.
### The first institutional scandals Trust in the supervisory authority was put to the test as early as the 1960s. On 4 June 1965, the Federal Council decided to dismiss Max Hommel, President of the CFB, with immediate effect. The accusation was serious: Hommel had provided paid advice to companies linked to the Spanish financier Julio Muñoz, involved in the Swiss regulatory developments have often encountered considerable internal resistance, reflecting a political culture that has long debated the appropriateness of stringent state regulation. An emblematic example of this opposition was recorded in May 1984, when a popular initiative aimed at imposing stricter controls on the sector was rejected by the electoral body with 73% of "no" votes. This result has consolidated, for decades, an approach based on self-regulation or targeted interventions only in cases of systemic emergency, rather than on constant proactive and sanctioning supervision.
### The comparison between past and present The current parliamentary debate on the new competences to be attributed to Finma proposes the same historical fractures. While the government intends to endow the authority with modern powers, such as the power to impose fines and to make public the name of defaulted institutions, Parliament shows a prudence that has its roots in 1916, the year in which the first bill remained stuck in the drawers for almost twentyyears. The fundamental difference today lies in the overall weight of the Swiss financial centre. If in the past the Trujillo banking scandal or the 1977 crisis were matters managed internally with discretion, the collapse of Credit Suisse has highlighted how the absence of immediate pressure tools prevents Finma from acting with the necessary timeliness.

IN BRIEF - The SSIC requests the abolition of penalties for delays in construction sites caused by heat. - The heatwave is not considered equivalent to bad weather and lacks compensation. - The Commission of the Council of States considers the parliamentary motion outdated.
KEY FACTS - **What**: Petition for fair conditions in construction sites during heatwaves - When: Parliamentary initiatives between December 2024 and March 2025 - Where: Construction sites throughout Switzerland - Who: Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) and Parliament - Amount: Contractual penalties of unspecified amount
During weeks characterized by intense heatwaves, the construction sector in Switzerland faces complex challenges related both to worker safety and to meeting project deadlines. The Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) has launched a petition aiming to request the introduction of fair and realistic framework conditions for managing work during extreme temperatures, asking that construction companies are not contractually penalized for the unavoidable delays caused by the heat.
The call for protection and clear rules In the petition, the SSIC emphasizes the urgent need to ensure effective protection of the health of construction workers. Contractors request that realistic deadlines are set for the completion of works and that transparent and uniform rules are established in cases where work must be suspended due to high temperatures.
Unlike what usually happens with adverse weather events or bad weather, interruptions and delays caused by extreme heat are rarely considered in construction contracts. Currently, such circumstances do not benefit from specific compensation, leaving companies exposed to high financial penalties in case of failure to meet agreed deadlines. Since heatwaves cannot be predicted or controlled by either companies or workers, the SSIC considers it unfair to fully burden builders with the economic consequences of these natural events.
Furthermore, the need to adhere to very tight contractual deadlines risks increasing operational pressure on personnel, directly jeopardizing the physical safety of outdoor workers under the blazing sun. Companies seeking to protect their staff by suspending work face potential economic damage related to the enforcement of penalty clauses. To understand the economic context of wages in the sector, it is possible to consult the details on the [Swiss payslip](nav:payslip) and related national parameters. ### The parliamentary framework and the position of the committees
The issue of protection against risks related to extreme temperatures at construction sites has been a topic of discussion within the federal Parliament as well. A pending motion requests the Federal Council to adopt appropriate measures so that natural influences are obligatorily included in planning and executing construction work. The text provides that, in the presence of extreme heat, construction companies should have the option to temporarily suspend activities to protect employees' health, without facing the threat of contractual penalties.
This motion had received support from the National Council, which approved it in December 2024. The parliamentary branch expressed the intention to establish explicit legislative protection for companies and workers.
### The position of the Council of States and the Committee
In March 2025, the Committee for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States announced its opinion on the parliamentary act. While sharing the fundamental objectives related to safeguarding health and ensuring fair working conditions, the Committee pointed out that the situation is already being managed. In line with the position expressed by the federal government, it was clarified that several measures have been initiated within a roundtable involving all relevant social partners in the sector.
Consequently, the Committee recommended that the plenum of the Council of States reject the motion, considering it effectively outdated by ongoing negotiations between employers and workers' representatives. The evolution of the debate highlights how much the issue impacts the [labour market](nav:jobs) and the organization of construction sites in Switzerland.
The discrepancy between the position of the National Council and that of the Committee of the States reflects the complexity of balancing production needs, contractual responsibilities of the client, and the duty to protect workers exposed to severe weather conditions.

For construction companies and workers, the immediate priority is to adopt internal preventive measures and adjust working hours during the summer months. Currently discussed practices include reorganizing shifts during the cooler parts of the day, setting up adequate shaded areas, providing refreshing drinks, and temporarily halting the most strenuous tasks when temperatures exceed safety thresholds.

The residence permit system in Switzerland comprises different types established by federal authorities, including the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), and implemented at the cantonal level. Understanding the distinction between categories L, B, and C is essential for those intending to settle or work in the country, considering that Switzerland is not a member of the European Union or the European Economic Area, although it applies specific bilateral agreements. Regulations precisely define access requirements, validity periods, and renewal procedures for each type of document issued to foreign citizens. Administrative management directly involves the population services of the various Cantons, which verify the applicant's economic, work, and housing conditions at the time of the initial application and during subsequent renewal deadlines. To learn more about the financial situation and deductions applied to salaries during the stay, you can consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) available online. ### The characteristics of short-term L permit
The L residence permit is intended for foreign citizens who have a fixed-term employment relationship, usually ranging from a few months to a year. This authorization is issued based on a specific employment contract, and its validity is strictly linked to the duration of the employment itself. Renewal of the L permit depends on the continued existence of the same employment conditions and does not automatically guarantee a transition to long-term residence categories. Procedurally, the employer or the worker must submit the required documentation to the cantonal migration office before starting professional activity on Swiss territory.
### The B residence permit for ordinary residence
The B residence permit represents authorization for ordinary residence, typically granted to those holding a permanent employment contract or a contract of at least one year's duration. The validity of this document is generally one year for third-country nationals and can be extended to five years for beneficiaries of the free movement agreements, depending on nationality and professional status. Holders of the B permit are required to comply with specific communication obligations in case of change of address or employment, promptly informing the relevant cantonal authorities. Unlike permit B, permit C is not tied to an annual expiry date and provides the holder with greater legal and economic stability, including exemption from certain restrictions regarding employment changes or independent activities. item.description: Complete guide to tenant's rights in Switzerland, security deposit, cancellation procedure and rental dispute.

## In brief - Know the rules regarding security deposits and notice periods in Switzerland. - Verify the correct procedure for contesting the initial rent. - Discover the cantonal differences applicable to residential leases. - Follow the regulatory steps to protect your tenant rights.
## Key facts - **What**: Rights and obligations of tenants in Swiss leases - When: Throughout the entire duration of the lease - Where: Across the entire Swiss territory and in various cantons - Who: Tenants, landlords, and competent conciliation authorities - Amount: Security deposit up to a maximum of three months' net rent
The Swiss real estate market is regulated by precise federal and cantonal laws that define the legal framework for residential lease agreements. When renting an apartment in Switzerland, it is essential to thoroughly understand the regulations regarding notice periods, security deposits, and rent disputes to avoid legal conflicts with property owners or property management. These provisions apply uniformly at the federal level but have operational specifics related to different cantons. The Federal Statistical Office (BFS) regularly monitors the cost of living and rental prices, providing useful data to assess the appropriateness of the requested amounts.
### The security deposit and banking rules Swiss law provides that the tenant may deposit an amount as security for contractual obligations up to a maximum of three months' net rent. This amount cannot be handed directly to the landlord but must be obligatorily deposited into a dedicated security deposit account opened in the tenant's name at a bank. This measure protects the tenant from improper use of the money and ensures that the interest accrued on the capital remains the property of the tenant throughout the lease duration. For more details on liquidity management and related accounts, see our [banking services](nav:banks).
### Contesting the initial rent A fundamental right recognized by Swiss law concerns the possibility to contest the amount of the initial rent within a strict thirty-day period from the delivery of the property, if the amount is deemed abusive or generates excessive returns for the landlord. This verification is based on the criteria established by the Code of Obligations and considers the local real estate market context, the condition of the property, and the periodically published reference interest rates. Practical analysis of termination procedures and deadlines Terminating a lease in Switzerland requires strict adherence to specific timeframes and formalities to avoid tacit renewal of the contract or the charging of unjustified monthly payments. The tenant's notice must be drafted exclusively in writing and signed by all parties listed on the lease agreement. In the case of an apartment occupied by a couple, the termination letter must bear the signatures of both spouses or registered partners, otherwise it is null and void.
The notice periods vary depending on the canton and local customs, although the Swiss Civil Code provides a minimum general term of three months for unfurnished apartments, with contractual deadlines established in individual agreements or according to cantonal practices. If the tenant intends to vacate the property before the contractual expiry without incurring financial penalties, law requires the presentation of at least one suitable, solvent substitute candidate willing to take over under the same contractual conditions on the same date.
### Return of the premises and the inspection report At the time of vacating the property, the landlord and tenant jointly conduct an inspection of the premises to prepare the handover report. This document certifies the state of wear of the apartment and distinguishes normal signs of deterioration due to daily use from damages attributable to negligence or carelessness by the tenant. The signing of the report is binding for the subsequent release of the security deposit held at the bank. item.description: The OCST reports: from January 2026, border workers of the new border municipalities who choose the Omnibus Decree will pay 100% tax at source in Ticino, no more than 80%. Increased tax burden if you opt for the Italian substitute tax.

## In a nutshell - From January 2026, 100% tax at source for old border crossers of new municipalities who choose the Omnibus - Until 2025 they were taxed at 80% as new frontier workers - Those who opt for the Omnibus risk double taxation: 100% in Switzerland + quota in Italy - Time until the end of 2026 for a diplomatic solution between Italy and Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Change in tax rate at source from 80% to 100% for a specific category of frontier workers - When: From 1 January 2026 - Where: Canton Ticino - Who: Tax office at the source of Ticino, border workers residing in the new border municipalities - Amount: Full rate (tables A, B, C, H) instead of 80% reduced
The Tax Office at the source of the Canton of Ticino has communicated, as reported by the Ocst union on its website, that from January 2026 the so-called "old border workers of the new Municipalities" who will opt for the mechanism of the Omnibus Decree will be taxed in Ticino at 100%, therefore according to the ordinary tables A, B, C and H, and no longer at 80% as is the case for new border workers.
### Who are the workers involved The provision concerns workers who carried out activities in Ticino between 31 December 2018 and 17 July 2023 with daily return, maintaining tax residence in a municipality included within 20 kilometres of the border, but which did not appear in the old list of border municipalities of the Canton of Ticino. The Tax Office at source has decided to ### The change and its practical consequences According to the OCST, with the new arrangement, affected cross-border workers would face a crossroads with significant economic implications. If they choose to opt for the Omnibus Decree, they will have to pay 100% of the withholding tax in Switzerland (according to full tables) and, at the same time, an additional amount in Italy as a substitute tax. The overall tax burden would be higher than the current situation.
The alternative would be not to opt for the Omnibus and continue paying 80% in Switzerland, while being classified as 'new cross-border workers.' This second option would avoid the immediate increase but would categorize the worker as a 'new cross-border worker' by legal definition, which does not match their contribution history (being an 'old' cross-border worker by seniority).

The table highlights how the combination '100% in Switzerland + 25% in Italy' creates an imbalance compared to both the old classic cross-border workers (who pay only 100% in Switzerland) and their previous situation (80% + 25%).
### The OCST appeal and political timing The Ticino union emphasizes that there is time until the end of 2026 to rectify the situation, but a structural solution to avoid increased taxes requires intervention from the Italian government with Bern to definitively resolve this 'ambiguous' situation that has persisted for several years. The matter is therefore on the diplomatic table between the two countries, with workers awaiting regulatory clarity that has yet to arrive.
### What changes for the income declaration For affected cross-border workers, the choice between the two options will directly impact the preparation of the Italian tax return. Those opting for the Omnibus will need to indicate in box CE of model 730 (or Redditi PF) the Swiss withholding tax paid at 100% to claim the tax credit, while those remaining under the 80% regime will have a lower withholding tax amount to offset. The difference in Swiss revenue thus influences the amount of credit usable in Italy, with subsequent effects on the net IRPEF owed. The second pillar, known as professional pension or LPP, represents a fundamental pillar of the Swiss pension system together with AVS.
